abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel analytical framework that fundamentally reconceptualizes the relationship between physical layer characteristics and network layer optimization in wireless communication systems. Traditional approaches treat these layers as separate design spaces, leading to suboptimal resource allocation and performance degradation in heterogeneous networks. We propose a unified stochastic geometry framework that incorporates channel state information, traffic dynamics, and mobility patterns into a single analytical model. Our method employs convex optimization techniques combined with stochastic network calculus to characterize the trade-off surface between signal-to-noise ratio, throughput, and end-to-end latency across different wireless network topologies. The analytical framework reveals previously unidentified dependencies that emerge when physical and network layers are co-designed, demonstrating that joint optimization can achieve performance gains unattainable through independent layer design. Numerical results validate the theoretical predictions across multiple scenarios, including millimeter-wave cellular systems, ad hoc networks with dynamic topology changes, and hybrid satellite-terrestrial architectures. The proposed framework provides network designers with rigorous mathematical tools for evaluating cross-layer design trade-offs and enables systematic exploration of the design space that was previously accessible only through simulation. This work establishes a new paradigm for analytical research in wireless network performance evaluation, with implications for next-generation mobile networks and beyond-5G system design.

This paper presents an enhanced analytical approach to modeling quality of service in multi-tier cellular systems, addressing critical limitations in existing queuing-theoretic models that fail to capture the complexity of modern wireless resource management. Conventional analysis based on classical Erlang models assumes homogeneous traffic and static resource allocation, resulting in significant inaccuracies when applied to cellular networks with diverse service classes and dynamic spectrum sharing. We extend the matrix-analytic method framework by introducing a Markov-modulated fluid process that accurately represents correlated traffic patterns and time-varying channel conditions in cellular systems. The proposed analytical model captures the interplay between new call arrivals, handover traffic, and adaptive modulation schemes, providing closed-form expressions for blocking probabilities and delay distributions. Numerical evaluation demonstrates that our approach achieves prediction errors below 5% in realistic deployment scenarios, representing a substantial improvement over existing approximations that exhibit errors exceeding 25%. The analytical framework enables network operators to perform efficient capacity planning and admission control optimization for quality of service provisioning. Furthermore, the model supports systematic investigation of the impact of various system parameters, including cell breathing effects, load balancing strategies, and fractional frequency reuse patterns, on overall network performance and service differentiation.

This paper presents AirMesh, a novel programmable data plane architecture designed for next-generation wireless mesh and sensor networks. Existing approaches rely on static protocol stacks that cannot adapt to changing application requirements or network conditions, resulting in either over-provisioned resources or quality of service failures. AirMesh introduces a fundamentally different architecture based on composable processing primitives that can be dynamically reconfigured at runtime. The system decomposes network functionality into modular processing elements that can be combined and parameterized through a declarative control interface, enabling fine-grained adaptation without service interruption. Each node implements a lightweight virtual execution environment optimized for the resource constraints of wireless devices, supporting both traditional routing operations and in-network processing for emerging applications. The control plane leverages intent-based programming to translate high-level network objectives into optimized data plane configurations, automatically handling the complexity of wireless-specific challenges including link variability, interference, and topology changes. We implemented a fully functional prototype on commodity hardware and evaluated its performance through extensive experiments in indoor and outdoor testbeds. Results demonstrate that AirMesh achieves competitive forwarding performance while enabling unprecedented flexibility, with configuration updates completing in under 50 milliseconds across networks of 100+ nodes. This work establishes a new architectural paradigm for wireless network protocol design.

This paper presents SmartMAC, an enhanced MAC protocol that significantly improves quality of service and security provisioning in wireless LAN systems through machine learning-based adaptation. Traditional IEEE 802.11 contention-based mechanisms struggle to meet the diverse QoS requirements of modern applications while maintaining robust security guarantees, often sacrificing one objective for the other. SmartMAC introduces a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework where individual stations learn optimal channel access policies based on observed environmental feedback. The protocol simultaneously optimizes throughput allocation, latency guarantees, and security enforcement by integrating intrusion detection capabilities directly into the MAC layer decision process. Our design maintains full backward compatibility with the 802.11 standard while introducing a lightweight learning plane that operates alongside the conventional contention mechanism. The learning agents employ a novel reward shaping technique that balances individual station performance with network-wide efficiency, preventing the emergence of selfish behaviors while encouraging cooperative optimization. Comprehensive simulation and testbed evaluations demonstrate that SmartMAC achieves 23% higher aggregate throughput and 41% reduction in delay variance compared to legacy 802.11 DCF under realistic traffic conditions. The security enhancement module successfully detects and mitigates jamming attacks and spoofing attempts with 94% accuracy while maintaining false positive rates below 6%. This work provides a practical pathway to intelligent, secure wireless LAN systems.
